strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important inference-time problem: generation quality can vary substantially with the initial noise seed.
Using internal attention behavior to rank seeds is an intuitive, potentially useful alternative to hand-designed frequency or temporal priors, and it requires no model retraining.
The evaluation generates 4,730 videos per configuration and reports results for both CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B.
The paper includes useful ablations on acquisition functions, candidate-pool size, stochastic sample count, layer truncation, temporal scope, and reversal of the selection criterion.
The method provides modest improvements over random seed selection with substantially less overhead than full best-of-N generation.
weaknesses: The core mathematical presentation is internally inconsistent. Equations 4 and 8 define mean entropy minus entropy of the mean, which is non-positive, whereas the implementation uses its non-negative negation. The supplement incorrectly claims that negating the score leaves its ordering and minimization behavior unchanged; it actually reverses the ordering. Under the main-paper equations, minimizing selects maximal rather than minimal disagreement.

The Bayesian interpretation is weak. The method does not define or approximate a posterior over model parameters, and independently masking fixed attention logits is not established as epistemic uncertainty. The paper itself concedes that BANSA is not derived from a Bayesian posterior.

The Bernoulli masking operation multiplies logits by zero before softmax rather than masking entries with negative infinity. Consequently, a masked logit becomes zero and can receive substantial probability, so this is not standard attention dropout and its behavior depends strongly on logit scale and sign. This design lacks theoretical or diagnostic validation.

The main comparison is only against a single random seed. Relevant noise-initialization and inference-time seed-selection baselines are omitted, yet the paper claims comparable or superior performance to them. The stated lack of official CogVideoX support does not justify making this comparative claim without experiments.

Reported gains are small, particularly the 0.25 total-score gain for CogVideoX-5B, and no confidence intervals, paired bootstrap tests, or repeated-trial variance are provided. Thus, statistical reliability is unclear despite the large number of generated videos.
Generality is overstated: both evaluated backbones belong to the same CogVideoX family. Claims about various architectures or broad generalization are unsupported.

The layer-selection procedure is described inconsistently. The main text selects depth by correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, whereas the supplement says correlation is computed with official quality scores after averaging across seeds. The latter may also introduce benchmark leakage if the same VBench prompts contribute to evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project-page link is blank, code and the complete prompt list are only promised for future release, and essential details such as attention type, head/layer aggregation, masking implementation, and memory management are insufficiently specified.

Claims that memory usage is unchanged and that overhead is measured in denoising steps are not substantiated; computing multiple dense masked attention maps may require appreciable memory, while the table appears to report wall-clock time without units or hardware-protocol details.
Qualitative comparisons show selected examples and sparse video frames without a blinded human study, making them inadequate evidence for motion and temporal-coherence claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant problem: video quality can vary substantially with the initial noise seed, and inexpensive seed ranking could be useful at inference time.

Using internal attention behavior to rank seeds is an intuitive model-aware alternative to handcrafted frequency priors. The method requires no retraining and reports moderate runtime overhead rather than multiple complete generations.

The evaluation generates 4,730 videos per configuration and includes several informative ablations, including entropy and dropout alternatives, ensemble size, candidate-pool size, truncated versus full-layer scoring, temporal scope, and reversed seed ranking.
Results improve all aggregate VBench metrics on both CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B, while the qualitative examples illustrate some plausible improvements.
weaknesses: The central mathematical definition is internally inconsistent. Equations (4) and (8) define BANSA as mean entropy minus entropy of the mean, which is non-positive; minimizing it favors greater disagreement. The appendix states that the implementation instead uses the opposite, non-negative BALD convention, but incorrectly claims that negating the score preserves its ordering under minimization. It reverses the ordering. Consequently, the stated method and implemented method select opposite seeds.

BANSA does not capture both confidence and consistency as claimed. Identical uniformly distributed attention maps have a zero score despite being maximally diffuse. The zero-score proposition establishes agreement only, not sharpness, confidence, generation quality, or semantic alignment.

The Bayesian and epistemic-uncertainty interpretation is inadequately justified. Bernoulli masks applied to fixed attention logits are artificial perturbations rather than samples from a parameter posterior. Moreover, Equation (7) multiplies masked logits by zero before softmax instead of excluding them with negative infinity, so the operation is not conventional attention masking and can assign substantial probability to purportedly masked entries.

The empirical gains are small, especially for CogVideoX-5B (+0.17 quality and +0.25 total), yet the paper provides no confidence intervals, variance across seed pools, paired tests, or statistical-significance analysis. The number of generated videos alone does not establish that these differences are reliable.

The most relevant prior methods, FreeInit and FreqPrior, are omitted. Claims of comparable or superior quality and approximately 64% lower cost are therefore unsupported. The study also lacks strong compute-matched alternatives, an oracle best-of-10 upper bound, and direct seed-level rank correlations between BANSA and final quality.

Both evaluated backbones are sizes of the same CogVideoX family. This does not support claims of generalization across various architectures. Figure 6 even refers to three models while displaying only the two CogVideoX variants.

The layer-selection description is contradictory: the main text defines the cutoff through correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, whereas the appendix says it correlates cumulative scores with official quality scores after averaging across seeds. The latter may also tune the method on VBench evaluation categories, with no clearly separated validation and test protocol.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Essential details such as attention type, head/token aggregation, precise timestep, masking reuse, baseline seed pairing, and repeated-run protocol are unclear; the project link is blank and the full prompt list and code are deferred to a future release.

Efficiency and qualitative claims are overstated. Runtime rises by 8.68% and 13.78%, contradicting statements of little to no increase, while unchanged memory is not demonstrated. Selected qualitative examples cannot establish temporal coherence from a few frames and are vulnerable to cherry-picking. Overall, the promising heuristic is not supported by a technically consistent formulation or a sufficiently controlled evaluation for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important inference-time problem: generation quality can vary substantially with the initial noise seed.
The model-aware use of internal attention signals for seed selection is interesting and reasonably novel relative to externally imposed frequency or temporal noise priors.
Evaluation is conducted at meaningful scale, with 4,730 generated videos per configuration on both CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B.
ANSE consistently improves VBench quality, semantic, and total scores while adding only 8.7%–13.8% reported inference time.

Useful ablations examine the acquisition function, ensemble size, candidate-pool size, layer truncation, temporal scope, and reversal of the selection criterion. The reversal experiment particularly supports the empirical usefulness of low implemented BANSA scores.
The method requires neither retraining nor an auxiliary quality model, and the paper discusses failure cases rather than claiming that uncertainty perfectly predicts perceptual quality.
weaknesses: The main BANSA definition has the wrong sign relative to the implementation. Equation 4 defines mean entropy minus entropy of the mean, whereas the supplement implements the opposite, non-negative BALD/Jensen–Shannon form. The supplement incorrectly claims that negating the score preserves its ordering under minimization; it reverses the ordering. This directly affects the stated selection rule and must be corrected throughout.

BANSA does not measure both confidence and consistency as claimed. A score of zero establishes agreement among stochastic attention maps, but identical high-entropy or uniform maps also attain zero. Thus, the proposition does not justify the claimed attention confidence or sharpness.

The Bayesian interpretation is weak: the Bernoulli masks are not samples from a parameter posterior, and element-wise multiplication of attention logits by zero is not conventional attention masking because masked logits still receive softmax probability. The paper needs stronger justification for why this perturbation represents epistemic uncertainty rather than an effective empirical heuristic.

The primary comparison is only against vanilla random-seed generation. Direct comparisons with prior noise-selection or optimization methods are omitted, and there are no matched-compute alternatives such as early-preview, reward-model, or CLIP-based candidate selection. Consequently, relative effectiveness is not established.

The reported improvements are modest, especially for CogVideoX-5B (+0.25 total VBench), yet no confidence intervals, repeated-trial variability, or significance tests are provided. The protocol also does not clearly explain how the 4,730 outputs and candidate pools are paired across methods.
Both evaluated systems belong to the same CogVideoX family, so claims of generalization across architectures are unsupported.

The layer-selection account is internally inconsistent: the main text and Figure 5 describe correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, while the supplement describes correlation with official quality scores after averaging across seeds. The latter could also introduce evaluation-set leakage if the same VBench prompts inform layer selection.

Important implementation details remain underspecified, including attention-head aggregation, treatment of different token or attention types, exact masking mechanics, timing units, and whether all ablations use the full benchmark. These issues limit reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important and underexplored problem: inexpensive, training-free selection of initial noise for text-to-video diffusion.
ANSE is evaluated on a broad range of backbones, including AnimateDiff, CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, and Wan2.1, with automated metrics, a user study, qualitative examples, and several ablations.
The proposed early-step and truncated-layer implementation has modest reported runtime overhead, and the reverse-score control provides some evidence that the ranking signal is meaningful.

The manuscript is generally well organized and explicitly discusses limitations. weaknesses: The central formulation is internally inconsistent with key ablations. Under Eq. 6, K=1 makes BANSA exactly zero for every seed and therefore cannot rank candidates, yet Table 8 reports a meaningful K=1 result without explaining tie-breaking. Likewise, with masks sampled as Bernoulli(p), p=0 produces all-zero rows that cannot be renormalized, while p=1 yields identical unmasked maps and zero BANSA; nevertheless, Table 10 reports distinct selection results at both endpoints. This suggests that either the method is implemented differently from its definition or the reported experiments are invalid.

The Bayesian and epistemic-uncertainty interpretation is unsupported. The stochastic maps are generated by externally masking one deterministic attention map, not by sampling a parameter posterior or stochastic model. The resulting Jensen-Shannon divergence primarily measures sensitivity to artificial masking and attention concentration; the paper provides no derivation showing that it estimates epistemic uncertainty.

The layer-selection procedure is contradictory. Section 3.3 defines the threshold using correlation between truncated and full-layer BANSA rankings, whereas Appendix D says BANSA scores are averaged over seeds and correlated with official quality scores. These are different procedures, and the latter may tune the method using evaluation labels. Dataset separation and reuse of prompts for selection, ablation, and final evaluation are not specified.

The statistical analysis does not substantiate significance. Ten random subsets of 100 videos from one generated collection are described as independent runs, paired tests are absent, many confidence intervals overlap, and some reported intervals are impossible for bounded metrics (e.g., Human Action extends above 1). Several dimensions also decline, contrary to the claim of consistent improvement.

There are serious reporting anomalies: HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 have exactly identical baseline and ANSE values across five metrics in Tables 5 and 19, despite being different models. This highly unlikely duplication undermines confidence in the results.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of BANSA from generic best-of-ten inference-time selection. FreqPrior is tested only on AnimateDiff, while stronger compute-matched selectors using CLIP alignment, aesthetic/reward models, attention statistics, or generated-output scoring are absent. Increasing denoising steps from 50 to 60 is not an adequate compute-matched baseline.

The gains are often small or mixed: CogVideoX-5B improves only 0.19 total VBench points, and several quality/semantic dimensions deteriorate. Evaluation of the newest backbones omits semantic scores. The user study lacks tie handling, uncertainty, significance tests, and a coherent explanation of how baseline and selected outputs can use 'identical noise seeds.'

Qualitative results are selected examples from a ten-seed pool and therefore do not independently establish superiority. Code, exact seed lists, complete prompt lists, and sufficient implementation details are unavailable, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The manuscript studies a practically relevant problem: inexpensive inference-time selection of initial noise for text-to-video diffusion.
The proposed selector is retraining-free, and the paper reports runtime overhead across several heterogeneous backbones.
The evaluation is broad in appearance, covering VBench, FVMD, a human study, qualitative examples, and ablations over candidate-pool size, masking probability, layer truncation, and temporal scope.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is technically incorrect. BANSA is a Jensen-Shannon disagreement measure, not a joint measure of confidence and consistency: identical diffuse or uniform attention maps receive the same zero score as identical sharp maps. Proposition 1 therefore establishes agreement, not the claimed certainty or generation quality.

The Bernoulli construction is not a Bayesian or epistemic-uncertainty approximation. It masks a deterministic attention map after computation rather than sampling model parameters or a posterior; the paper provides no derivation connecting this artificial sensitivity measure to epistemic uncertainty.

Several reported experiments are incompatible with the equations. With K=1, Eq. 6 is identically zero for every seed and cannot rank candidates, yet Table 8 reports meaningful K=1 selection results. Under the stated mask definition, p=0 produces all-zero rows that cannot be normalized, while p=1 produces identical unmasked samples and a zero score; nevertheless, Table 10 reports nontrivial selection results at both endpoints.

The human-study protocol is impossible as written. It claims that baseline and ANSE outputs use identical noise seeds, but seed selection is the only operation ANSE performs. With the same model, seed, and sampling settings, the two outputs should be identical. If different seeds were actually used, the protocol and pairing must be explained, and the claimed preference results cannot presently be audited.

The quantitative reporting contains major internal inconsistencies. HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 have exactly identical values for five of six metrics in Tables 5 and 19, including matching confidence intervals in Table 19, despite being different models. Values for CogVideoX also differ between main-paper and appendix tables. These patterns strongly suggest copying or aggregation errors.

The statistical analysis does not substantiate the claims. Confidence intervals from ten random 100-video subsets are not an appropriate paired significance analysis; many intervals overlap, several metrics decrease, and no paired tests or confidence intervals on method differences are supplied. Nevertheless, the paper asserts statistical significance and consistent improvement.

The comparison is not compute- or selection-matched. ANSE chooses one candidate from ten, whereas the baseline is a single random seed. The equal-compute control merely adds denoising steps to a sampler not calibrated for them, rather than comparing against ten random generations, best-of-N reranking using standard video-quality or reward models, or relevant seed-optimization methods such as InitNO.

The layer-selection description is contradictory: the main text defines correlation between truncated and full-layer scores across seeds, whereas the appendix says scores are averaged across seeds and correlated with official quality scores. It is also unclear whether selection hyperparameters were tuned on evaluation prompts.

Core reproducibility details are missing, including handling of fully masked rows, attention-head/token aggregation, the exact masking convention, tie-breaking for degenerate scores, precise prompt splits, and released code. The project-page reference is blank.

Because the central acquisition function is mischaracterized, multiple ablations contradict its mathematical definition, and the human and quantitative evaluations contain serious validity problems, the main claims are not currently trustworthy. strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important problem: generation quality varies substantially across initial noise seeds, and selecting a seed using only an early denoising step is potentially valuable.

ANSE is simple, training-free, and broadly applicable. Evaluation spans several substantially different video-diffusion backbones, including AnimateDiff, CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, and a preference-aligned model.

The empirical study is unusually broad, including VBench, FVMD, human preferences, runtime measurements, qualitative comparisons, correlation analysis, reversed-score controls, and ablations over candidate-pool size, ensemble size, masking probability, attention type, layers, timesteps, and CFG.
The reported efficiency is appealing: approximately 9–16% inference overhead is considerably lower than iterative noise-refinement methods, while the AnimateDiff results show meaningful gains.

The negative correlations between BANSA and several quality measures, together with degradation when selecting the highest-BANSA seed, provide useful evidence that the score contains predictive signal.
The presentation is generally clear, with an intuitive motivation, a straightforward algorithm, an explicit limitation discussion, and extensive qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central Bayesian/confidence interpretation is not technically established. Equation 4 is a Jensen–Shannon-type disagreement among artificially masked versions of one deterministic attention map, rather than uncertainty under a posterior over model parameters. Bernoulli masking therefore does not directly estimate epistemic uncertainty in the BALD sense.

BANSA measures disagreement but not necessarily confidence: identical uniformly diffuse attention maps have BANSA zero and would be considered optimal, despite being maximally entropic. This directly weakens the repeated claim that a low score guarantees both confident and consistent attention.

Most improvements on the strongest models are small and sometimes mixed. CogVideoX-5B gains only 0.19 in total VBench score, while some individual metrics decrease; HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 also show regressions in aesthetic quality. The evidence supports modest average improvement more clearly than consistently better generation.

There are troubling reporting inconsistencies. HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 have exactly identical baseline and ANSE values for five metrics in Tables 5 and 19, which appears unlikely and needs verification. One confidence interval exceeds the valid metric range, and the claimed statistical validation uses overlapping random subsets rather than clearly defined independent experimental units or paired significance tests.

The layer-selection description is internally inconsistent. Section 3.3 defines the criterion as correlation between truncated and full-layer BANSA scores, whereas Appendix D says it correlates cumulative BANSA with official quality scores after averaging over seeds. This affects both reproducibility and the possibility of evaluation-set tuning.

The baseline study is incomplete for an inference-time selection paper. It lacks stronger compute-matched alternatives such as selecting among the same candidates using inexpensive latent, attention-entropy, or pretrained reward/quality predictors, as well as a clearer comparison to best-of-N generation under an equal wall-clock or FLOP budget.

The statistical protocol is underspecified: it is unclear how prompts, repetitions, and seeds are paired; whether uncertainty includes prompt-level variation; and whether the correlation and hyperparameter-selection prompts are disjoint from evaluation prompts. Overlapping confidence intervals also do not substantiate several stated improvements.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The project-page location is blank, code and complete prompt lists are only promised for future release, and implementation details needed to reproduce masking, attention aggregation, layer choices, and runtime accounting are incomplete.

Overall, the idea and experimental breadth are promising, but the conceptual overclaiming and reliability issues in the evaluation keep the paper slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold in its current form.
